checks.label: Twelve screens: five that show and seven puzzles, alternating to the ninth and ending on three mixed puzzles
Each line sits 440 ÷ 1.732 = 254 V from the star point; six feeders of 3 MΩ make 500 kΩ, and of 120 kΩ make 20 kΩ
Dry, the dial reads 500, 250, 115, 28.3, 0.998 and 0 kΩ with no fault and with a 500, 150, 30 or 1 kΩ or a solid fault
Lamps cannot see an equal fall on every phase: with Damp everywhere and no fault, all three lamps read 254 V while the dial reads 20 kΩ, below all three alarm levels
A solid fault puts out its own phase's lamp and lifts the other two to 440 V, on every phase, damp or dry
At 1 µF a phase, a 30 kΩ fault on L1 gives lamps of 254, 248 and 261 V; a 1 kΩ fault gives 190, 256 and 420 V
Three phases of 1 µF at 60 Hz look like 1 ÷ (2π × 60 × 3 µF) = 884 Ω to the hull, far less than a 30 kΩ fault
At DC the capacitance drops out: the settled reading is 28.3 kΩ for a 30 kΩ fault at every capacitance from 1 to 10 µF
Ships' mains alarm should the insulation resistance fall below 50 ohms per volt of the operating voltage: 22 kΩ on 440 V, so 1 kΩ alarms and 30 kΩ does not
The response value should be set to approx. 100 Ω/V: 44 kΩ on 440 V
A typical critical insulation value is 500 ohms/volt: 220 kΩ on 440 V
A 28.3 kΩ reading alarms at 100 and 500 Ω/V but not at 50 Ω/V; a 115 kΩ reading alarms only at 500 Ω/V
Paths in parallel read below the lowest one: every fault, damp or dry, reads below both the fault and the feeders together
Worked numbers: 500 + 150 = 650 kΩ; 50 ÷ 0.1 = 500; feeders of 2,000, 2,000, 1,000 and 40 kΩ read 37 kΩ together
The dial settles in five time constants, in proportion to the capacitance: 5 µF a phase takes five times as long as 1 µF
Switching on Damp everywhere: the lamps stay equal at 254 V all the way, while the dial falls below its alarm line within 3 s
Screen 5 settles the dial once at 1 µF, then five times as slowly at 5 µF, and everything settles within 5 s
A move Dan makes changes the picture in 0.3 s, and at 1 µF the dial settles within 0.6 s
Before an answer, no puzzle's picture shows its result
The right answer sits first, second or third across the puzzles, never in one place throughout
